sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(One note for the director, not filed here because no line in this section covers it: the page has one heading over a single 15-line paragraph, at roughly x 120–680, y 120–550. That paragraph holds five separate topics: when the boat runs, boarding, bicycles, tickets and passes, and winter hours and notices. Someone looking for one answer, such as "can I bring my bike?", has to read the whole block. The heading itself passes WCAG 2.4.6 because it does describe the page. The missing subheadings and chunking belong to the hierarchy, arrangement and text sections.)

**What's working.**
- **Nothing is there for show.** There are no rules, boxes, badges or decoration. A bold heading and plain body text in one sans-serif family and one near-black give the piece a single calm, practical mood that suits a public-service notice.
- **The copy reads well.** Every sentence says who does what and when ("Foot passengers board first, from the ramp on the upstream side"). Numbers come with their units and reference points ("every forty minutes", "about twelve minutes in calm weather"), and nothing is placeholder or misspelled.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director: none of this section's lines is a `no`, but the hierarchy stops at the title. The body (x 120–678, y 125–550) is one 15-line block that covers five separate topics: the timetable, boarding order, bicycles, tickets and winter service. There are no subheadings and no paragraph breaks. A passenger looking for one fact, such as "can I bring my bike?" or "when is the last winter boat?", has nothing to land on below the title and has to read from the top. This page is for looking things up, so the missing second level probably does the most damage of anything on it. I filed nothing here because the checklist puts paragraph and heading structure inside running text under the text and arrangement sections. Make sure one of those critics raises it. The fix is to split the block into short sections with bold run-in labels or small headings (Times, Boarding, Bicycles, Tickets, Winter).

**What's working.**
- The title (about 36 px bold, near-black, y 60–100) is clearly larger, heavier and darker than the body text (about 18 px regular). The eye knows where to start, and the two levels differ in both size and weight, not in size alone (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8).
- There are only two type sizes and the step between them is big, so neither one looks like a mistake (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** The body text (x≈120–680, y≈125–550) is one unbroken block of about 15 lines holding five separate topics:
   - crossing times (lines 1–4),
   - boarding order (lines 4–5),
   - bicycles (lines 5–9),
   - tickets and the season pass (lines 10–12),
   - winter service and printed timetables (lines 12–15).

   Every line gap is the same, about 27 px, so space shows no groups at all. Someone who came to check whether they can bring a bike, or where to buy a ticket, has to read from the top to find it. That is the job this page fails. The heading-to-body gap (about 30 px) is fine. The fault is inside the body.
   - **Why:** Equal gaps everywhere erase the groups (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II; Wertheimer 1923).
   - **Fix:** Break the block into one short paragraph per topic, with a gap between paragraphs clearly larger than the line spacing. Short subheads or bold run-in labels ("Bicycles", "Tickets", "Winter") would make each topic findable at a glance. Defect. Weight: **major**.

2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip? / Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over? / Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion?** (One problem, three lines.) All the content sits in the upper-left 560 × 490 px of a 1280 × 800 frame. There is about 120 px of margin on the left, about 600 px of empty space on the right, and about 250 px empty below. The space is gathered, but nothing shows it was chosen. Nothing on the right balances the dense dark block on the left, and the 120 / 560 / 600 split follows no proportion. The viewer reads it as an unstyled or half-loaded page rather than a designed notice, and that weakens trust a little. It does not stop anyone reading.
   - **Why:** A heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, ch. I "Balance"). Large unexplained empty areas are a fault (Tschichold, *The New Typography*; Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*). The proportion point is a soft guide only (Elam), so treat it as taste.
   - **Fix:** Either make the asymmetry look meant, by setting the column on a stated grid with a deliberate margin ratio, or use the right side for something that earns it. A small at-a-glance panel would work: frequency, crossing time, last boat, where to buy tickets. That would also help with finding 1. Centring the column is the fallback, but it only hides the problem. Convention (balance, negative space) plus taste (proportion). Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.** The heading and body share one exact left edge at x≈120, and the heading sits closer to the body than to anything else. The single column also keeps the measure readable, so the reading path runs cleanly from heading to body with no competing elements.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (space inside groups smaller than between; empty space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances; main divisions follow one proportion).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists?** No. Everything below the heading is one unbroken paragraph of 16 lines, at about x 120–678 and y 125–550. It covers at least five separate topics:
   - the schedule and crossing time ("every forty minutes", "about twelve minutes")
   - boarding order (foot passengers first, from the upstream ramp)
   - bicycle rules (wait at the gate, lower deck, lock to the rail, keep bags on, leave the stairs clear)
   - tickets and the season pass
   - the winter timetable and where printed timetables are kept

   A passenger who only wants one fact, like "can I bring my bike?" or "when is the last boat in winter?", has to read from the top to find it. Nothing marks where a topic starts. Times and conditions that people act on are buried mid-line: "one boat each hour" and "before dusk" sit at y≈458. This is a convention: people skim screen text, and a long dense block defeats that (Nielsen, "How Users Read on the Web", Nielsen Norman Group, 1997). Here the cost is real, because the page is reference information that people dip into, not something they read once from start to finish.

   Fix: split the text into short sections under small subheads, roughly Timetable, Boarding, Bicycles, Tickets, Winter. Set the bicycle steps as a short list, since they are a sequence of instructions. Keep the type, size, measure and leading as they are, because they already work. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The setting of the text itself is sound. Lines run about 60–66 characters, inside Bringhurst's 45–75 range. Leading of about 1.5 suits that measure, the rag is gentle (627–677 px) with no staircase, and the last line is full, not a lone word. Once the block is split, every chunk will read comfortably.
- There is one family with a clear two-level contrast: a heavy, slightly tightened heading over a regular-weight body in near-black on white. Contrast is comfortably high and nothing competes with the text.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists)

Here's the walk through the colour checklist.

First read: the eye lands on the bold near-black heading at the top left (120–595, 55–100), then drops into a dense grey-black paragraph. The right half of the page is empty. It reads as a plain information page for ferry passengers. It feels calm and plain.

The job, as I assume it: a web page of practical notes that passengers read for times, boarding and tickets.

Colour walk:
- Small palette: yes. It uses only white and near-black.
- Strong colour kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated colour at all.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white has full value contrast, and the heading is a little darker and heavier than the body.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. The body text is one even tone throughout.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colours: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. Colour carries no meaning.
- Dark theme: yes. It is not a dark theme.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is neutral only: near-black type on a white page.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The body copy looks like a soft near-black rather than pure #000 on white. That keeps contrast well above 4.5:1 without the harsh glare that makes a long, unbroken paragraph like this one tiring to read. The heading looks a little darker than the body, and weight and size do the rest, so the page's one level of structure still shows clearly in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon, logo or mark, only a heading and one paragraph of body text on white.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The text column takes about the left 680 px. The right half of the frame (x ≈ 700–1280) and the strip below the text (y ≈ 560–800) are empty white.
